title: Preference-Guided Adversarial Policy Optimization for Long-Tail Robust Driving
claim: Training is a zero-sum game whose inner adversary loop and outer defender loop are coupled through one shared objective.
layout: Central game box with attacker and defender panels left and right, loop modules below
description: A symmetric, cartoon-styled diagram built around a central blue box titled 'Zero-sum Markov Game', which holds the max-min expected discounted return objective. A pink knight sits to its left and a teal knight to its right. The left panel is the attacker side. It has a pink 'Attacker's Return' slider, a road scene with pink adversarial trajectories, crossed swords and a bar chart labelled G_psi. The right panel is the defender side. It has a teal 'Defender's Return' slider, a road scene with a teal trajectory fan, a shield and a Gaussian labelled pi_theta. A teal 'Outer Loop' arc above the box carries a policy-gradient formula. A pink 'Inner Loop' arc below the box leads to three boxed modules: Return Est., Sampling and Dist. Match (solved via IPL), each with its equation and a small icon.
caption: Illustration of ADV-0. It alternates between an Inner Loop where the adversary ψ evolves via IPL to track the failure frontier, and an Outer Loop where the ego πθ optimizes policy gradients against the induced adversarial distribution.
abstract: Deploying autonomous driving systems requires robustness against long-tail scenarios that are rare but safety-critical. While adversarial training offers a promising solution, existing methods typically decouple scenario generation from policy optimization and rely on heuristic surrogates. This leads to objective misalignment and fails to capture the shifting failure modes of evolving policies. This paper presents ADV-0, a closed-loop min-max optimization framework that treats the interaction between driving policy (defender) and adversarial agent (attacker) as a zero-sum Markov game. By aligning the attacker's utility directly with the defender's objective, we reveal the optimal adversary distribution. To make this tractable, we cast dynamic adversary evolution as iterative preference learning, efficiently approximating this optimum and offering an algorithm-agnostic solution to the game. Theoretically, ADV-0 converges to a Nash Equilibrium and maximizes a certified lower bound on real-world performance. Experiments indicate that it effectively exposes diverse safety-critical failures and greatly enhances the generalizability of both learned policies and motion planners against unseen long-tail risks.
